newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-GERMANY WAS NO FOOTBALLING HOME FOR KLINSMANN.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-GERMANY WAS NO FOOTBALLING HOME FOR KLINSMANN.

text.p: Juergen Klinsmann returned to his native Germany hoping to a put down roots after a career abroad as the country's "footballing diplomat".
But Germany's captain rarely felt at home at Bayern Munich with its scandals, squabbling and defensive tactics.
Friday's announcement that the striker is packing his bags again to join Italy's Sampdoria next season came after a turbulent two seasons in Munich.
It all started with great hope and ended with a rare burst of public anger from a man usually known for his cool and diplomacy.
After making his name at Stuttgart Kickers and VfB Stuttgart, Klinsmann first tried his luck abroad with Internazionale Milan in 1989, just a few weeks after helping VfB to the UEFA Cup final.
His travels took him to the French first division with Monaco (1992-1994) and England with Tottenham (1994-1995) before he returned to Bayern at the start of the 1995-1996 season.

His ability to learn foreign languages helped him become a popular figure in the game across Europe. Although the forward did have problems with both tactics and trainers in Italy and France, Klinsmann always left a good impression abroad.
He enjoyed the greatest popularity of his career during just one season in England when he was voted Footballer-of-the-Year after overcoming a reputation in the country for theatrics.
But despite his success, the 32-year-old left Tottenham because he really believed the long-term future of both his career and private life was in Germany. It turned out to be a faulty decision.

At first Bayern chairman Franz Beckenbauer was regarded as having pulled off a major coup with Klinsmann's signature. Thousands of Bayern fans turned out to watch his first training session in July 1995.

But as time went on Germany's most prominent player was often at the centre of controversy and criticism. His poor relationship and public disputes with club captain and former World Cup hero Lothar Matthaeus did not help his cause.

Klinsmann hated the squabbling in the Bayern dressing rooms which is part of everyday life in Munich. This season the defensive tactics of Italian coach Giovanni Trapattoni frustrated the player intensely.
Klinsmann's feelings boiled over last weekend when he kicked in an advertising sign after being substituted during a league game, leaving the field shouting and cursing.
The decision to move to Italy, however, seems to have a great deal to do with his personal as well as his professional life.
Klinsmann and his American wife Debbie have just had their first child. They are both said to enjoy staying at their house near Lake Como in northern Italay.
Sampdoria should also provide the player with the regular first-team football which he needs to make sure of his place as captain of the national team at next year's World Cup finals.

He was linked with more glamorous clubs such as Real Madrid where competitive for places is fierce. But Klinsmann knows he is approaching the end of his career and must be sure of his spot in the team.
The move to Italy is likely to be the last major European transfer of the player's career. Klinsmann, who turns 33 in July, is expected to sign a one-year contract.
After the 1998 World Cup, the striker is expected to retire from international football and finish his career in the United States.
